newsitem.title: CROATIA: Differences persist despite US pressure on Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Differences persist despite US pressure on Croatia.

text.p: The United States piled pressure on Croatia on Tuesday, saying future relations will depend on whether Zagreb meets all its post-war commitments under a peace accord it signed in 1995.

President Bill Clinton's special envoy, Robert Gelbard, met with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb on Tuesday and raised "all the concerns the United States has been raising with the government of Croatia for some time".

Under the Dayton peace treaty Croatia has nominally agreed to allow all refugees, including up to 200,000 Croatian Serbs, to return home and to cooperate with an international war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
"Croatia must permit the return of all refugees, and this means all Croatian Serbs who wish to return to their homes in Croatia must be able to do so," Gelbard told a news conference.
But he said talks with the 75-year old nationalist president left much to be desired, although Tudjman expressed his willingness to be "supportive".
"There is still a fundamental difference of views between us but we'll continue to stress it. This issue will be fundamental in our bilateral relations," the diplomat told reporters.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright lambasted a visiting Croatian delegation in Washington two weeks ago over the country's treatment of minority Serbs who are unable to return or are subject to harassment once they are back.
Tudjman said on Sunday Croatia was ready to tackle the return of Serb refugees who are in Eastern Slavonia but rejected as unreasonable Western demands for Croatia to take back all the Serbs.

Eastern Slavonia is the last Serb enclave in Croatia, now administered by the United Nations, where there are some 60,000 Serb refugees from their former rebel state of Krajina, recaptured by Croatian troops in summer 1995.

"No one in my country has tried to limit this rate to only Serbs in Eastern Slavonia. Serbs currently in Yugoslavia and Bosnia must be able to (return) as well, as is required by the Dayton agreement and international law," the diplomat said.

"Obstacles such as law on temporary takeover of property must be removed," he said, referring to a law Croatia passed after up to 200,000 Serbs fled the Krajina to regulate the status of their abandoned houses.

Zagreb says Serb property has been confiscated temporarily and will be returned to owners once they return. But many Serb houses were in practice soon occupied by Croat refugees expelled by Serb nationalists from nearby Bosnia.

Gelbard also said Croatia had "clear-cut obligations" to cooperate with The Hague tribunal trying those accused of war crimes during the 1992-1995 war in former Yugoslavia. Of the 15 indicted Bosnian Croats, Zagreb recently extradited one, while another surrendered voluntarily to the tribunal over a year ago.

Zagreb claims all the other indictees are outside Croatia and out of reach of Croatian police, although at least one was known to have been in Croatia since his indictment. Gelbard said Croatia must ensure "all indictees who enter its territory are apprehended and turned over. We also expect Croatia will use its influence to press for the turnover of Bosnian Croats living inside Bosnia".

"We don't limit our demands only to Croatia," said Gelbard, who also raised the issue with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday. "It's a fundamental issue on which we will judge our relations with any country that has any relations to indicted war criminals," he said.
"We have a variety of means, including economic leverage, to ensure compliance is achieved," he said.
